name: Brow dyeing blonde / bleaching

lead: Bleaching or dyeing the brows lighter, often blonde, softens the face or makes a distinct style statement. The colour change is visible right away. Dyes can also be used to darken brows instead.

Hydrogen peroxide with an alkaline agent oxidizes melanin in the hair, lightening it, with home products typically around 6 percent peroxide and salon products up to 12 percent. It is common hair-bleaching chemistry, and no studies of brow bleaching specifically were found.

paras: People go to a salon or use an at-home kit, applying product to the brows for a set time before rinsing. The shade fades or grows out over weeks, and roots may need touch-ups.

Irritation, allergic reactions (including to phenylenediamine dyes, which can appear hours or a day later), breakage and discoloration are documented with hair coloring in general. The skin around the eye is sensitive.

angle.text: People bleach or dye their brows lighter, often blonde, to soften the face or make a style statement. The peroxide lightens the brow pigment, so the colour change is visible right away. It uses standard hair-bleaching chemistry.

lead: Brow bleaching lightens the eyebrow hairs, anywhere from a shade or two to blonde, platinum or near white, to change how the face reads. People use it to match brows to lighter hair, to soften strong dark brows, or to create a bold, editorial look that contrasts with dark hair.[1][2] Dermatologist Hannah Kopelman describes the effect in beauty-press coverage as either bold or softer depending on the wearer's hair colour.[2]

The lightening works through oxidation: hydrogen peroxide, made alkaline by an additive such as ammonia or monoethanolamine, breaks down melanin, the pigment that gives hair its colour. Home kits typically contain around 6% peroxide, and salon products somewhat more.[3][4] Brow-specific products are formulated for the area, and hairstylist Ashleigh Marie Rancilio says head-hair bleach is too strong for it.[2] Bleached brows are reported to stay light for about four to six weeks before regrowth shows darker roots.[2]

The opposite adjustment, tinting brows darker with a dye close to the hair-on-the-head colour, is a long-standing option for sparse or pale brows, alongside pencils, gels, microblading and transplants.[1][5] Wikipedia's hair-bleaching article dates the fashion-world interest in bleached eyebrows to the early 1990s, with a wider spread in the late 1990s and early 2000s and a return in the early 2020s.[4]

No clinical trials of brow bleaching have been published. Dermatologists quoted in beauty coverage and the US FDA's hair-dye guidance describe the main risks as skin irritation, allergy, thinning hair and eye injury.[2][6]
infobox: Cosmetic colour treatment for eyebrow hair

paras: Brow bleaching lightens the pigment in the eyebrow hairs, while brow dyeing deposits colour, usually to darken pale or sparse brows toward the colour of the hair on the head [1][3]. Fashion coverage describes bleached brows on runways during Fashion Month, in editorial work, in costume and special-effects makeup, and in everyday style, with some wearers aiming for platinum and others going only slightly lighter than their natural colour [2]. A related look, sometimes called the invisible brow, uses very pale or white brows [2].

Bleached hair of any kind often passes through warm stages as it lightens. Wikipedia describes black hair moving through brown, red, orange and yellow before reaching pale yellow, and toners, such as violet products that counteract yellow, are used afterwards to shift brassy undertones.[4][3] Users in looksmaxxing forums describe the same stage: one poster bleaching his hair said that after toning it 'actually looks white now' and that he saw little visible outgrowth because his hair was already light blond.[7]

Eyebrows are prominent in facial expression, and researchers have argued that communication, not only keeping sweat and debris out of the eyes, is their main function.[1] Because brow colour changes how strongly the brows frame the eyes, lightening them changes the visual contrast of the upper face. Kopelman describes the effect as bold and edgy against dark hair, or softer against light hair.[2]

People with blonde or light hair may bleach brows so that they match, since dark brows against pale hair can look heavy. Others with dark hair use the contrast deliberately for a high-fashion look.[2] The change is immediate and, because it only affects the hair, it grows out without any lasting alteration to brow shape.[2][4]

Hair lightening is old. Wikipedia notes that in the 1st century BC Diodorus Siculus described Celtic men washing their hair in lime to make it blond, and that Romans used ash-based solutions that often caused hair loss. Hugh Plat's 1602 book described a sulfuric acid treatment, and lye and sun exposure were common but hazardous methods in early modern Europe.[4]

Modern peroxide-based colouring developed from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The hair-colouring article credits Eugene Schueller, founder of L'Oreal, with the first synthetic hair dye in 1907, and Schwarzkopf with the first home colour product in 1947.[3] The 1931 film Platinum Blonde helped popularise platinum hair in the United States, and in 1950 Clairol introduced a one-step lightening dye.[4]

Brow fashion has swung widely. Eighth-century Japan favoured hikimayu, in which natural brows were shaved or plucked and redrawn higher on the forehead; Elizabethan high-status women sometimes removed their brows; and the 1920s and 1930s favoured thin, plucked, pencil-line brows. Thick brows later became associated with Audrey Hepburn.[1]

Bleached eyebrows entered the fashion world in the early 1990s and became more widely known in the late 1990s and early 2000s before returning in the early 2020s.[4] Beauty coverage in 2023 described bleached brows as a regular sight on runways and among celebrities, and said the look had spread to people doing it at home after seeing it on TikTok.[2]

Hair bleaching oxidises melanin. Commercial formulas usually pair hydrogen peroxide with persulfate salts under alkaline conditions, and the oxidation is not easily reversed, which is why lightened hair stays light until it grows out.[4] Home products typically contain about 6% hydrogen peroxide, while salon products can contain more.[4]

Dyeing differs from bleaching. Permanent hair colour contains ammonia and a developer and lifts natural pigment; demi-permanent colour uses a milder alkaline agent and a lower-strength developer and deposits colour without lightening; semi-permanent colour has no developer and cannot lighten; temporary colour coats the surface and washes out.[3] Brow tinting darker typically relies on these deposit-type dyes, and Wikipedia notes that permanent dye similar to hair dye is often used to darken brows.[1]
Brow-specific bleach products are formulated for use near the eye, and Rancilio says solutions made for the brows should be used rather than head-hair products.[2]

In beauty-press interviews, dermatologist Marisa Garshick recommends a patch test on the inner arm and a barrier such as petroleum jelly around the brows, and Kopelman advises giving brows time to recover between sessions.[2] Aftercare suggestions in the same coverage include a brow serum and moisturiser, avoiding harsh actives such as retinol, and sun protection.[2] Results are described as lasting about four to six weeks, after which roots show with regrowth; touch-ups are optional and brows can otherwise grow out to their natural shade.[2]

Availability from professionals depends on location. The same article reports that salons in California cannot offer the service because of a state rule about products the FDA has not approved, that New York stylists may use only demi-permanent dyes on brows, and that many brow studios do not offer bleaching. At-home facial bleach kits are the alternative, and the article advises following the pack directions exactly.[2]

Tinting darker, brow pencils, shaders, gels, powders and eyeshadow are the long-standing ways to define or fill sparse brows.[1] Hair removal methods such as tweezing, waxing, threading and trimming shape the brows; threading, which originated in India and Iran, became popular in Western countries from the late 1980s.[1][8]

Microblading, a semi-permanent tattoo technique that adds hair-like pigment strokes by hand, began as a medical camouflage for hair loss, grew as a cosmetic procedure in the 1980s and 1990s and became popular in Singapore by about 2007 and in North America by the mid-2010s. Wikipedia says it can last up to two years, and notes that in the United States it is not federally regulated.[5] Eyebrow transplants move follicles, most often from the back of the head, to sparse areas.[1]

Garshick warns that repeated chemical processing can thin brow hairs and that bleach can cause redness or lighter or darker skin patches, which may be more noticeable on darker skin.[2] Rancilio states that using the wrong product near the eyes risks blindness, and bleach in the eyes is described as the most serious hazard.[2] Wikipedia's hair-bleaching article adds that persulfate-containing products can cause allergic and irritant contact dermatitis, swelling and hives.[4]

The FDA states that eyebrow and eyelash dyeing are not permitted uses of coal-tar hair dyes, that these dyes carry label wording that they must not be used on the eyelashes or eyebrows, and that hair dyes have caused eye injuries, including blindness, when used in the eye area. It advises a patch test on the skin before each use of hair dye, notes that a passing test does not guarantee that no reaction will follow, and says PPD has been implicated most prominently in allergic reactions.[6] Reactions to hair colour may not show until hours or a day later, and some European dermatologists have cautioned that pre-use patch testing can itself sensitise.[3]

Brow bleaching is discussed in appearance forums mostly as part of wider hair-lightening and contrast discussions, rather than as a dedicated protocol. Posters describe lightening as permanent in the sense that it must grow out, report that results depend on how light the starting colour is, and describe hair texture changes from long processing.[7] Fashion and beauty media, rather than forums, are the main source of coverage for brows specifically.[2][4]

No studies found on brow bleaching specifically. Peroxide bleaching has been studied extensively on teeth, where reviews describe the oxidation mechanism and sensitivity effects [9][10], but those findings concern a different tissue and use.

lore.intro: Bleached brows are discussed in fashion coverage and on social video, with beauty professionals and dermatologists offering the main expert commentary, while appearance forums mostly discuss hair lightening in general.[2][7]
